title: Numbers, age & quantities
goal: Count things and people, ask how much and how many, give your age and use ordinals from first to tenth.
intro:
First learn the numbers from the **Numbers** chart: 1–10 are essential, and the teens are irregular (పదకొండు 11, పన్నెండు 12, పదిహేను 15). From 20 on the system is regular: tens + units, ఇరవై ఒకటి (21), ముప్పై ఐదు (35).

Telugu has a special set of numbers for **counting people**: *ఇద్దరు* (two people), *ముగ్గురు* (three people). And it distinguishes *ఎంత* (how much) from *ఎన్ని* (how many).

vocab.note: Joins with numbers: పదేళ్ళు (padēḷḷu), ten years.

phrases.en: Give me a little more, please.
How much does it come to in total?
Tell me your phone number, please.

grammar.title: Counting things and people
grammar.body:
**Things**: put the number before the noun, and use the **plural** noun for two or more: *రెండు పుస్తకాలు* (two books). For 'one', use the short form **ఒక** before a noun (*ఒక పుస్తకం*); **ఒకటి** is 'one' on its own (*ఒకటి ఇవ్వండి*, give me one).

**People**: Telugu uses special human numerals:
ఒకరు (1) · ఇద్దరు (2) · ముగ్గురు (3) · నలుగురు (4) · ఐదుగురు (5) · ఆరుగురు (6) · ఏడుగురు (7)
From about eight, use the ordinary number + **మంది** (mandi): ఎనిమిది మంది, పది మంది, వంద మంది.

With 'we' and 'you' the human numeral takes a person ending: *మేము ముగ్గురం* (there are three of us), *మీరు ఎంతమంది?* (how many of you are there?).

grammar.title: How much, how many, how old, which one
grammar.body:
**ఎంత** (enta) = how much (amounts, prices): *ఇది ఎంత?* **ఎన్ని** (enni) = how many (countable things). **ఎంతమంది** (entamandi) = how many people.

**Age** uses the 'I have' pattern: dative + number + **ఏళ్ళు** (years). The number and ఏళ్ళు often merge: పది + ఏళ్ళు → పదేళ్ళు, రెండు + ఏళ్ళు → రెండేళ్ళు.

**Ordinals**: *మొదటి* (first), then number + **-ō** in speech or **-va** in writing: రెండో/రెండవ, మూడో, నాలుగో, ఐదో, ఆరో, ఏడో, ఎనిమిదో, తొమ్మిదో, పదో (10th).

examples.en: How many books do you need?

dialogue.title: Planning a birthday
dialogue.setting: Asha and her mother plan her sixteenth birthday party.

lines.speaker: Amma
lines.en: How many people are coming to the birthday?

lines.speaker: Amma
lines.en: Then do we need two cakes?

lines.speaker: Asha
lines.en: No, Mum, one big cake is enough.

lines.speaker: Amma
lines.en: How old are you turning? Sixteen?

lines.speaker: Amma
lines.en: Already! Okay, what else do we need?

lines.speaker: Asha
lines.en: Some sweets and two litres of juice.

culture: Indian English and Telugu both count large amounts in **lakhs** (లక్ష, 1,00,000) and **crores** (కోటి, 1,00,00,000), not millions; prices and salaries are quoted this way. In shops, numbers are very often said in English, especially prices and phone numbers, so be ready to hear 'two-fifty' as readily as *రెండు వందల యాభై*. The sixtieth birthday (*షష్టిపూర్తి*) is a major family celebration.
